source: Holton, Mackridge & Philippaki-Warburton, Greek: An Essential Grammar, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2016), upload 418329ba, PDF pp. 22-44 = Ch. 4 (§4.1-4.10). Copyrighted, no open license: rules restated in own words; examples shortened; paradigms and word lists are linguistic facts. Separate from pronouns.json (another source).
overview: Pronouns stand in for noun phrases; determiners modify nouns (words other than articles, adjectives and numerals). Most Greek pronouns except personal pronouns can also be determiners. The book's Appendix 1 tabulates them (not in these pages).

weak_personal.rule: Weak (clitic) pronouns are one unstressed syllable pronounced together with the word they depend on (§1.8). There are no weak nominatives for 1st/2nd person since the verb shows the person; a strong pronoun is used for emphasis (§4.2). They are far commoner than strong pronouns.
notes: The 3rd-person nominative forms occur only in exclamatory and interrogative constructions after να 'there!' and πού 'ν' 'where is/are': να τη! 'there she is!', πού 'ν' τα; 'where are they?'.
Fem. pl. accusative τις/τες: τις is obligatory before the verb; either may follow a gerund or imperative.
functions: direct object (accusative) or indirect object (genitive) of a verb
genitive after an adjective, numeral, pronoun or quantifier
genitive after certain adverbs (mostly of place, §8.3)

rules: Nothing may come between a weak object pronoun and its verb.
Weak object pronouns stand immediately before the verb, except with imperatives and the gerund, where they follow it (and the verb takes a second stress, §1.8).
With two weak object pronouns the indirect (genitive) precedes the direct (accusative); after an imperative or gerund the order is flexible.
Colloquially σου may reduce to σ' before a 3rd-person pronoun: Σ' το είπα (sometimes written Στο είπα).
As possessive, the genitive normally follows the noun, which normally has the definite article (but see §3.54).
As possessive it may instead follow an adjective or the quantifier όλος.

After a comparative, the genitive weak pronoun gives the second term of comparison (μεγαλύτερή του; alternative: μεγαλύτερη απ' αυτόν); after a relative superlative it gives the group (η μεγαλύτερή μας).
After numerals, certain pronouns (compare §4.6, §4.9) and όλος it specifies the person: 1st, 2nd or 3rd.

examples.el: Ξεφυλλίζοντάς το, καταλαβαίνουμε ότι πρόκειται για αξιόλογο βιβλίο.
examples.en: Flicking through it, we realize it's a noteworthy book.

examples.el: Πες του το. / Πες το του.
Η Άννα είναι η μεγαλύτερή μας.
examples.en: Anna is the biggest/oldest of us.

strong_personal.rule: Strong (emphatic) pronouns inflect for number and case (3rd person also for gender). They distinguish one person from another; they can be subject, object, object of a preposition, stand alone, or accompany a noun phrase.
notes: 1st/2nd-person accusative forms lose their initial vowel after the prepositions από, για: για μένα 'for me'. The initial vowel of the 1st/2nd nominatives is often dropped in rapid speech after a word ending in a vowel (apostrophe): Ξέρω 'γώ.

3rd person = also the demonstrative 'this' (§4.3); declines like -ος, -η, -ο adjectives, except that final -ν is often added to masc. and fem. accusative singular. τούτος and εκείνος decline alike and can be 3rd-person pronouns too.
Colloquial alternative genitives of the 3rd person: masc./neut. sg. αυτουνού, fem. sg. αυτηνής, plural αυτωνών (all genders).

examples.en: (As for me,) I don't want to go.

demonstratives.rule: All decline like -ος, -η, -ο adjectives (§3.33). They are strong 3rd-person pronouns or true demonstratives, as pronoun or determiner. As determiner the noun must have the definite article and the demonstrative stands outside article + noun: demonstrative + article + noun for something present; in writing it may follow the noun when referring back. αυτός and εκείνος can head a relative clause.

examples.en: I want this one, not that one.

examples.el: Θυμάμαι το πρώτο μας σπίτι. Το σπίτι αυτό βρισκόταν στο κέντρο της πόλης.
examples.en: I remember our first house. This house was in the centre of town.

examples.el: Αυτός που ήρθε χθες ήταν περίεργος άνθρωπος.
examples.en: The one who came yesterday was a strange man.

examples.el: Εκείνοι που λένε τέτοια πράγματα θα έπρεπε να τιμωρηθούν.
examples.en: Those who say such things ought to be punished.

qualitative.rule: Pronoun or determiner; also in κάτι τέτοιο 'something like that'.

examples.el: Δεν είχαμε τέτοιους στα νιάτα μου.
examples.en: We didn't have people like that in my youth.

quantitative.rule: Pronoun or determiner. 'So much/many' can also be adverb τόσο + the appropriate form of πολύς, or both τόσος and πολύς are declined.

examples.en: Don't put in so much sugar!

possessives.rule: The weak genitive pronoun is the non-emphatic possessive (§4.1). Emphatic possessive δικός + weak genitive is both pronoun and determiner; it contrasts persons or emphasizes ('my own'). δικός agrees in gender, number, case with the thing possessed; declined like -ος, -η, -ο (§3.33), with colloquial feminine alternative δικιά (like -ος, -ια, -ο, §3.35). It takes the definite article in definite phrases and none in indefinite ones. Used attributively, predicatively or after a preposition.

examples.el: Το δικό μας σπίτι είναι παλιό.

examples.en: She hasn't got a house of her own.

examples.el: Το τελευταίο σπίτι είναι το δικό μας.
examples.en: The last house is ours (the one where we live).

examples.el: Το τελευταίο σπίτι είναι δικό μας.
examples.en: The last house is ours (it belongs to us).

examples.el: Πάμε στο σπίτι σου ή στο δικό μου;
examples.en: Shall we go to your house or mine?

interrogatives.rule: Three interrogative pronouns/determiners: ποιος 'who?, which?', τι 'what?' and πόσος 'how much?'. τι is indeclinable and modifies nouns of any gender, number or case. πόσος declines like -ος, -η, -ο (§3.33). ποιος declines like -ος, -α, -ο (§3.34) except masc. (sometimes fem. sg.) accusative adds -ν; extended genitives are colloquial.
interrogatives.note: For 'whose?' τίνος is often used instead of the genitive singular masc./neut. (not fem.); genitive plural τίνων (all genders). Direct and indirect question use: §10.6, §10.10.

indefinites.rule: Two kinds: specific ('someone', 'something') and non-specific ('anyone', 'anything', 'no one', 'nothing').

forms: κάποιος, -α, -ο (like §3.34 adjectives; masc. acc. sg. κάποιον)
specific.rule: κάποιος can be a determiner with nouns of any number, gender or case. κάτι can be a determiner with plural nouns of any gender/case meaning 'some'; it may be followed by determiners (κάτι άλλο, κάτι τέτοιο, κάτι δικό μου) or an adjective, which normally takes the article (κάτι το ωραίο).

notes: Fem. forms with stressed -ι- (καμιά etc.) are more emphatic.
Final -ν may be added to masc./fem. acc. sg. before a vowel or voiceless plosive; κανέναν is the normal masc. acc. sg. as pronoun (no noun).
Colloquially neuter κανένα may shorten to κάνα, only as determiner or in the compound καναδυό.

κανείς is also a slightly more formal alternative to κανένας, and (formal) means 'one' (indefinite subject in a non-negative clause), normally right after the verb; colloquial equivalent is 2nd sg. of the verb: Εύκολα βλέπει κανείς τα φριχτά αποτελέσματα του πολέμου.
non_specific.use: Used in questions, negatives and other non-assertive clauses (subjunctive, conditional, imperative). With a verb in a negative sense the verb needs δεν or μην. They can also stand alone as negative answers. In positive statements they mean roughly 'about one'. καμιά φορά = 'occasionally'; καμιά is used with approximate numerals (καμιά δωδεκαριά 'about a dozen', §5.4); καναδυό (colloquial, = κανένα δύο) 'one or two'. τίποτα can take determiners or an adjective: τίποτ' άλλο, τίποτα τέτοιο, τίποτα το ωραίο.

examples.en: I prefer you to say nothing.

examples.el: Ίσως να σε δει κανένας δάσκαλος.
examples.en: Perhaps a teacher will see you.

examples.el: Αν σε δει κανένας δάσκαλος, θα σε αναφέρει.
examples.en: If a teacher sees you, he'll report you.

particle_pou.rule: The basic relative is the indeclinable που: it does not agree with the noun and does not distinguish human from non-human. A Greek relative clause must begin with the relative word; unlike English it cannot be omitted as object. που can introduce any relative clause (§10.9).

examples.el: Ο άνθρωπος που ήρθε είναι ο αδελφός μου.
examples.en: The man who came is my brother.

examples.el: Ο άνθρωπος που είδες είναι ο αδελφός μου.
examples.en: The man (whom) you saw is my brother.

examples.el: Το δέντρο που φυτρώνει στην αυλή μου είναι πορτοκαλιά.
examples.en: The tree that is growing in my back yard is an orange.

examples.el: Το δέντρο που είδες είναι πορτοκαλιά.
examples.en: The tree (that) you saw is an orange.

ο οποίος.rule: The alternative, more complex relative: definite article + οποίος; both inflect for gender and number (agreeing with the modified noun) and for case (matching the function inside the relative clause). οποίος declines like -ος, -α, -ο (§3.34). Always has the article and is stressed on the last-but-one syllable. See §10.9.

correlatives_free_relatives.gloss: whoever (declines like §3.34; masc. acc. sg. όποιον; not to be confused with ο οποίος)
that which, what, whatever (comma distinguishes it from complementizer ότι and interrogative τι)
as much/many as, however much; (pl.) those which (declines like §3.33)

relatives.note: The correlatives are used as pronouns or determiners in free relative clauses that do not modify a noun (§10.9.2).

καθένας.gloss: every one, each one (mainly pronoun; inflected like ένας and κανένας)

universals.καθετί: 'each thing', indeclinable; both καθένας and καθετί may optionally take the definite article.
universals.κάθε: 'each, every': indeclinable determiner used with singular nouns only; the article is optional (§7.1 for time expressions).

examples.en: Each one of us knows it.

ίδιος.rule: Always with the definite article. As pronoun ο ίδιος means 'the same' or '(my)self'. As a determiner immediately before the noun it means 'the same'; when the article is repeated before the noun, or after a strong pronoun, it means 'myself/yourself' etc. Without the article ίδιος means 'identical, alike'.

examples.el: Θέλω να μιλήσω με την ίδια.
examples.en: I want to speak with her in person.

examples.el: Θέλω να μιλήσω με την ίδια τη Μαρία.
examples.en: I want to speak to Mary herself.

μόνος.rule: With or without a noun, typically 'only'. With a genitive weak pronoun it means 'by myself/yourself…' (without company or help).

examples.el: Ήταν ο μόνος φοιτητής που ήρθε.
examples.en: He was the only student who came.
He was the only one who came.

άλλος.declines_like: -ος, -η, -ο, with emphatic genitives: masc./neut. sg. αλλουνού, fem. sg. αλληνής, plural (all genders) αλλωνών
rules: May recur in one sentence for 'some… others…'.
After κάποιος, κανένας, ποιος, όποιος it means 'else': κάποιος άλλος 'someone else', κανένας άλλος 'nobody else', ποιος άλλος 'who else', όποιος άλλος 'whoever else'.
With a numeral it may precede or follow it with different meanings.
άλλος τόσος = 'as much again' (twice as much).
Reciprocal: ο ένας τον άλλο 'each other' (§10.24).

examples.el: Αν είχαμε άλλα τόσα λεφτά θα μπορούσαμε να αγοράσουμε το σπίτι.
examples.en: If we had twice as much money, we could buy the house.

quantifiers.rule: Quantifiers express quantity, not number. όλος 'all' and ολόκληρος '(the) whole' decline like -ος, -η, -ο (§3.33). With a noun they are accompanied by the article and stand outside article + noun (like demonstratives). Plural όλοι = 'everyone'/'all of them'; neuter όλα = 'everything'.

list.gloss: much, a lot of, too much; (pl.) many, too many; comparative περισσότερος 'more' (no distinction between much/many and too much/many)
the rest of (always with the article)
a whole load of (colloquial; indeclinable; originally acc. 'a pile')

quantifiers.note: All except ένα σωρό inflect like -ος, -η, -ο adjectives except πολύς (§3.38).

examples.en: A whole load of Italians came.

adverbs.gloss: very (with positive adjectives), much (with comparatives), a lot; comparative περισσότερο 'more'
a little, a bit; comparative λιγότερο 'less'
